clue.text: Army entertainer

definitions.meaning: a ... is a great multitude, especially an army, as in the heavenly ...
one who receives and entertains guests

explanation.definitionFit: Both senses are standard: a huge armed multitude, and the person who welcomes guests at a party.

clue.text: Peddle part made by plant

parts.note: to hawk goods is to peddle them
a bit is a part or piece

explanation.surface: Selling a share of the business made by a factory.
explanation.walkthrough: 'plant' reads as a factory but is a flower.
explanation.definitionFit: Hawkbit is a yellow-flowered weed of the daisy family, so it is a kind of plant.

clue.text: He's Fleet St's deeper sort

indicators.note: to sort is to rearrange, so these letters are put in another order

explanation.surface: A journalist on Fleet Street is a more profound kind of person.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fleet St' calls up London's old newspaper street; 'Fleet' is the adjective for quick, and 'sort' rearranges ST'S DEEPER.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone fleet of foot is fast, and a fast mover is a speedy one.

clue.text: As experiment it's nice if re-served cold

indicators.note: served up again, so these letters are dished out in a new arrangement

parts.note: C is the abbreviation for cold, as on a tap

explanation.surface: A dish that tastes nice reheated, or rather served cold, as a kitchen experiment.
explanation.walkthrough: 're-served' shuffles ITS NICE IF into SCIENTIFI, then C for cold goes on the end. 'As experiment' is adjectival: in the manner of an experiment.
explanation.definitionFit: An experiment is the hallmark of scientific method, so something done as an experiment is done in the empirical way.

clue.text: Encounter humour that's black, not lewd, ultimately

indicators.note: what is black replaces what is lewd, one letter swapped for another

parts.note: comedy is humour

indicators.note: ultimately points to the final letter of the word before

parts.note: B is the abbreviation for black, as on pencils

explanation.surface: Coming across black humour that stops short of being smutty.
explanation.walkthrough: 'not' swaps D, the last of 'lewd', for B in COMEDY.
explanation.definitionFit: To come by something is to obtain or chance upon it, so to encounter it.

clue.text: Mid-siesta? Leave the ironing —- I'll make coffee!

annotationWithheld.why: Mid-siesta? Leave the ironing — I'll make coffee! (8): ES (mid-siesta) + PRESS (ironing) gives ESPRESS, but no clue word fairly supplies the final O
annotationWithheld.clue: Mid-siesta? Leave the ironing —- I'll make coffee!

clue.text: Lines from Lear don't show fate, sadly, protecting a king

indicators.note: the shuffled letters wrap round the other piece to shield it
sadly means in a sorry state, so these letters are knocked out of order

parts.note: K is the abbreviation for king in chess

explanation.surface: Lear's tragic fate on stage is muted, though he is still guarding his crown.
explanation.walkthrough: 'sadly' signals the anagram and 'protecting' the wrap-around. King Lear is a red herring: this is Edward Lear the nonsense poet, and the poem concerns a ruler of Swat, in present-day Pakistan.
explanation.definitionFit: Edward Lear wrote the nonsense poem of that title, so it is a set of lines by him.

clue.text: Gold in Sunshine State leads to area's growth

indicators.note: one piece goes inside the other

parts.note: Florida's nickname is the Sunshine State, abbreviated Fla
or is gold in heraldry

explanation.surface: Finding gold in Florida leads to growth in the area.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sunshine State' is Florida, abbreviated FLA; OR (heraldic gold) goes in.
explanation.definitionFit: Flora is the plant life of a region, the vegetation that grows there.

clue.text: Cricketer from school shortly getting hundred

parts.note: comp is the short form of comprehensive school
a ton is a hundred, as in a century at cricket

explanation.surface: A cricketer straight out of school soon scores a century.
explanation.walkthrough: Denis COMPTON was an England batsman of the 1940s and 1950s; a 'comp' is a British state secondary school.
explanation.definitionFit: Denis Compton was a celebrated England batsman, so he is an instance of a cricketer.

clue.text: One ineffectual, if phenomenally unusual Beijing telephone directory?

definitions.meaning: a feeble, effete young man, usually upper-class

definitions.text: if phenomenally unusual Beijing telephone directory?
definitions.meaning: a list of Beijing names with no Chins in it would be a marvel

explanation.walkthrough: The British phrase means a weak, upper-class twit; the second reading jokes that a Beijing directory lacking the surname Chin would be a wonder.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom names a weak, ineffectual upper-class man, literally one lacking a strong jaw.

clue.text: King intervening in strike in town

indicators.note: one piece comes between the letters of the other

parts.note: wham is a heavy blow
Rex is Latin for king, as in royal signatures

explanation.surface: A monarch steps in to settle an industrial strike somewhere in a provincial town.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Strike' reads as a walk-out but is a blow. WREXHAM is a town in north Wales.
explanation.definitionFit: Wrexham is a market town in north-east Wales, so it is an instance of a town.

clue.text: Home, say, visited by judge or model early

indicators.note: the guests come into the host's house, so one piece goes inside the other

parts.note: Sir Alec Douglas-Home was a British Prime Minister, so Home is an example of a PM
a referee judges a match, shortened to ref
taken as written

explanation.surface: A house call from a judge, or someone modelling clothes, early in the day.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Home' looks like a house but is Alec Douglas-Home, British Prime Minister 1963-64; 'visited by' puts the judge and the 'or' inside him.
explanation.definitionFit: To preform is to shape something in advance, that is to model it beforehand.

clue.text: Press person in company to waste no time changing accommodation

annotationWithheld.why: Press person in company to waste no time changing accommodation (3,3,9): ED (press person) in BAND gives BEDAND, but no sound reading of 'to waste no time changing' gives BREAKFAST; no blog found to confirm the setter's intent
annotationWithheld.clue: Press person in company to waste no time changing accommodation

clue.text: Like posh fellow, perhaps, making bird glower

parts.note: a tit is a small songbird
read as 'one that glows', a light-emitting diode glows

explanation.surface: A posh chap who scowls at a passing bird.
explanation.walkthrough: 'glower' looks like a scowl but is one that glows: an LED.
explanation.definitionFit: A posh fellow may well be a lord or baronet, someone holding a title of nobility.

clue.text: A young male celebrity backed in concert

parts.note: a son is a young male offspring

indicators.note: this word is put in reverse, read from back to front

parts.note: a big name is a celebrity

explanation.surface: A young male star is supported at a live music event.
explanation.walkthrough: 'backed' turns NAME into EMAN; 'in concert' looks like a gig but means together.
explanation.definitionFit: Acting as one man means everyone acting together, which is what in concert means.

clue.text: Mistake comic actor for resident of Drury Lane

parts.note: to muff something is to bungle it, a mistake
John Inman was a British comic actor in Are You Being Served?

explanation.surface: Mistaking a comedian for someone who lives on a London theatre street.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Drury Lane' suggests theatre; the nursery rhyme asks 'Do you know the muffin man who lives on Drury Lane?'.
explanation.definitionFit: In the traditional nursery rhyme the muffin seller is said to live in Drury Lane.

clue.text: Start trouble when inviting bachelor to abscond

parts.note: to jump is to start with surprise
B is the abbreviation for bachelor, as in a BA
to ail is to trouble

explanation.surface: Starting trouble by asking a single man along before running off.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Start trouble' reads as stirring things up, but each word is a separate piece; 'inviting' signals the insertion.
explanation.definitionFit: To jump bail is to fail to appear in court after release, running away from justice.

clue.text: Way of building traditions that Parisian follows

parts.note: mores are the customs and conventions of a society
que is French for that, as a Parisian would say it

explanation.surface: Building traditions observed by someone from Paris.
explanation.walkthrough: 'follows' places the French word after the customs; 'Way of building' is an architectural style, not a construction method.
explanation.definitionFit: Moresque is the Moorish style of architecture and ornament, so it is a way of building.

clue.text: Bubbly fellow's eating very soft little sweeties

indicators.note: one piece takes the other inside it

parts.note: Moet, the champagne maker, with the possessive S
pp, pianissimo, is the musical mark for very soft

explanation.surface: A cheerful man is munching some very soft little sweets.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bubbly' reads as cheerful but is champagne, named after its maker; 'eating' signals the musical mark going inside.
explanation.definitionFit: Moppets are small children, often called sweeties as a term of endearment.

clue.text: Exchange racket before smashing

parts.note: a racket is a swindle or con
fab, short for fabulous, means smashing or great

explanation.surface: A tennis racket handed over just before someone hits a smash.
explanation.walkthrough: 'racket' and 'smashing' paint tennis; they are a swindle and a word of praise.
explanation.definitionFit: A confab is an informal chat, an exchange of talk.

clue.text: State line dividing Russia and America

indicators.note: the line splits the other piece in two

parts.note: the bear is the traditional emblem of Russia
US is short for United States, that is America

explanation.surface: A border line separating Russia from the United States.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Russia' is its national emblem, the bear, not an abbreviation; 'dividing' means the line splits it, and America follows.
explanation.definitionFit: Belarus is an independent state in eastern Europe, a country bordering Russia.

clue.text: Beneath lettuce, spider regularly develops habit of crawling?

indicators.note: in a down entry the next piece sits below the first

parts.note: cos is a crisp variety of lettuce

indicators.note: taking every other letter of the word

explanation.surface: A spider under a lettuce leaf takes to crawling.
explanation.walkthrough: 'regularly' takes S, I, E from SPIDER under COS. COSSIE is British and Australian slang for a swimsuit; the crawl is a stroke.
explanation.definitionFit: A habit here is clothing, and one worn for swimming the crawl is a swimming costume.

clue.text: Kipling story-teller can cultivate foppish look, with luck

indicators.note: to cultivate is to work over and develop, so these letters are worked into a new order

explanation.surface: With luck, a man might adopt a dandyish appearance.
explanation.walkthrough: 'can cultivate' reworks FOPPISH LOOK and LUCK. Puck tells the children the old stories in Kipling's book of that name.
explanation.definitionFit: In Kipling's book the sprite Puck, from Pook's Hill in Sussex, narrates English history to two children.

clue.text: For crunch match initially loading dice

indicators.note: the cut-up item is loaded with another letter inside it

parts.note: to dice food is to chop it

indicators.note: initially picks the first letter of the word

explanation.surface: Before the decisive game, someone is weighting the dice.
explanation.walkthrough: 'dice' reads as gaming cubes but is to cut up; 'loading' puts M inside CHOP. 'crunch match' is a red herring.
explanation.definitionFit: To chomp is to munch noisily, to crunch food with the teeth.

clue.text: Starts to lecture sexy, sordid gal on stripping

indicators.note: stripping takes the outer layer off each word, leaving its inner letters

explanation.surface: A lecture opens on a lurid tale of a girl taking her clothes off.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Starts to lecture' looks like the first letters of 'lecture' but is the definition; 'stripping' takes the outsides off SEXY, SORDID and GAL.
explanation.definitionFit: Exordia are introductory parts of a discourse or treatise, the openings of a lecture.

clue.text: His unwanted messages, returned in part, scar Emma psychologically

indicators.note: returned says the hidden letters are read backwards
in part says the answer is a run of letters hidden inside the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: Someone's nasty letters, sent back, have left Emma with emotional scars.
explanation.definitionFit: A person whose unwanted messages flood inboxes is the sender of junk email.

clue.text: Extra-fast using the tube?

parts.note: read as a quick London Underground trip, but fast means firmly stuck, and the tube is the adhesive's container

explanation.definitionFit: Something stuck with a strong instant adhesive from a tube is fixed extra fast.

clue.text: African runners appear, as anthem may be over

indicators.note: turned over, so the word is read backwards

parts.note: an anthem is usually sung

explanation.surface: Athletes from Africa line up while the national anthem finishes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'over' turns SUNG round; 'runners' are not athletes but animals that run.
explanation.definitionFit: Wildebeest are African antelopes that run in great herds, hence runners.
